Figure 2:Two stages, one interface.Top: the task input and robot interface shared by both stages (observations, physical actions, memory and files, history). Left,Evaluate(first-attempt round K0): one in-context episode of observe–reason–act through the shared tools, with no workspace; history and notes stay inside the episode. Right,Optimize(self-improvement rounds K1–KHH): each round runs from a persistent workspace of skills, tools, policy and memory, is graded natively, revised with robot actions closed, and committed as the start of the next round, until the first native success or the round limit.

Figure 3:Difficulty-balanced task sampling.Three tasks per difficulty stratum, from D1 (highest official RoboDojo success rate) to D6 (lowest), covering RoboDojo’s five official task categories. Strata are assigned by ranking the tasks on the official RoboDojo success rate[3]and are fixed before the main evaluation; they do not describe the subsequent refinement outcomes.

Figure 4:Capability associations and the barrel hypothesis.The matrix reports exploratory rank associations across six systems on the 18 tasks. Each barrel represents one RSI axis, with a stave per capability group. Stave heights illustrate a proposed bottleneck interpretation of the associations.

images.caption: Figure 9:Cross-task workspace transfer.Top: original self-improvement trajectories for tasks first solved at K6 or later. Bottom: trajectories initialized from a workspace pooled from all other tasks, excluding the target task. First success advances from K9 to K1 for Sonnet 5.5 on Cover Blocks, from K14 to K7 for Opus 5.5 on Organize Table, and from K15 to K8 for Opus 5.5 on Deposit Coin. These examples illustrate faster adaptation with transferred workspaces. Red crosses indicate unsuccessful attempts, dark checks mark first success, and pale checks carry success forward without additional evaluation.
